ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits the ground identified since **1841** as the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, held by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. **Ari fróði** put that þing on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, fourteen kilometres away, and nobody has ever closed the gap. The old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it. (More on parliaments shortly.)

ctx: the point of the block — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: Þingvellir wasn't Kjalarnes moved house — it was something new and national. Kjalarnes just proved Icelanders could hold a parliament without a king.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: The Parliament Before the Parliament

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** — son of **Ingólfur Arnarson**, Iceland's first settler — held the **Kjalarnesþing** before the national **Alþingi of 930**. Our only near-contemporary source is **Ari fróði**, writing around **1122–33**: *"en áðr var þing á Kjalarnesi"* — before that, the þing was on Kjalarnes. Tradition even credits Þorsteinn with **consecrating** that later national parliament — so the founder's son didn't just build the prototype, he blessed the sequel.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: **Here's the catch: nobody has ever found it on Kjalarnes.** **Jónas Hallgrímsson** went looking in **1841**, examined **Leiðvöllur** on the farm **Esjuberg**, and decided it was a footpath. The national register still lists that spot as *sést ekki* — nothing to see. What he found instead was **14 km away, at Þingnes on Elliðavatn**: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring 43 feet across** with a heap of stones in the middle. He proposed that was the Kjalarnesþing, and in **1930** the state made it official — the protection order calls Þingnes *hinn forni Kjalarnessþingstaður*. **Thirteen ruins are protected there today**, last surveyed in **June 2025**. The join between Ari's Kjalarnes and Jónas's Þingnes has **never been proven** — so Iceland's first parliament is a place we can name and can't quite find.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / ⚖️ Kjalarnesþing
en: Nothing was written down — Iceland had no writing worth the name — so **Úlfljótur carried the whole code home inside his head.** He was sent **shortly before 930** and spent **three winters** in Norway, landing home in time for the founding of the **Alþingi in 930**. What he recited is **Úlfljótslög**, the oldest law this country has. Úlfljótur supplied the text. Þingvellir only supplied the venue.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
en: **Ragnheiður Gíslason** and **Þórarinn "Þóri" Jónasson** moved onto the run-down farm in **1967** and started the riding business in **1968**, after a visitor asked out of nowhere whether they'd take him out on horseback. Six horses, summers only. It grew into **Iceland's oldest continuously running riding-tour company** — **120 horses** and around **15,000 riders a year** by **2018**, **85% of them from abroad**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
en: Their horses work on screen too. The Mosfellsbær local paper *Mosfellingur* puts it plainly: **"hestar frá Laxnesi birst í nokkrum bíómyndum eins og Game of Thrones"** — horses from Laxnes have appeared in several films, *Game of Thrones* among them. In **1992** Þóri shipped Icelandic horses to the **United States** to show them off near Hollywood and ended up on **CBS and CNN**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🎬 Laxnes Horse Farm
en: And the name. **Halldór Guðjónsson** was raised on this farm from the age of **three**. When he started publishing he took the farm's name — **Laxness** — and in **1955** that name won Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature**. The house he built, **Gljúfrasteinn**, is **600 metres further up the valley**: our next stop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn
en: The typist was **Auður Sveinsdóttir**, born at **Eyrarbakki on 30 July 1918**, and she didn't just type it — she ran the build. She married **Halldór Laxness** that **Christmas Eve, 1945**. The architect was **Ágúst Pálsson**; the house was home from **1945** until Halldór died on **8 February 1998**. Auður outlived him by fourteen years, dying **29 October 2012**, aged **94**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn
en: **1955:** Halldór takes Iceland's **only Nobel Prize in Literature** — *"for his vivid epic power which has renewed the great narrative art of Iceland."* Auður marked it the way a textile artist would: she made **Maríuklæðið**, "Mary's Cloth", to commemorate it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Þingvellir / 🪶 Gljúfrasteinn
en: The **Icelandic state bought the house and its art in 2002**, a hundred years to the year since Halldór was born, and opened it to the public on **4 September 2004**. His **typewriter is still on the desk**.

en: Iceland Through the Years

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **ACT I — Borrowed clothes.** Iceland still working out who it sounds like. Five of the biggest singalongs here are secretly Anglo-American hits in Icelandic disguise — *Mambo Italiano*, *California Dreamin'*, *I Will*, Ray Sharpe rockabilly, and a Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm. The mambo arrived secondhand, via 1950s Manhattan. Post-war crooners, dancehall ballads, and Keflavík kids who saw The Beatles in Bournemouth and ran home to start a band.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **01 · Jeg vil ha' morfor med mig ud på sjov** — *Raquel Rastenni*. Plot twist — the Danes nicked it. The song is actually “Jag ska' ta' morfar med mej ut i kväll,” a 1949 Brita Borg banger out of Stockholm, dressed up in a Danish coat a year later. Same writers (Peter Spar / Jessup Sandy), different *morfar*.  [Secret-cover thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **02 · Litla flugan** — *Sigfús Halldórsson*. Iceland's most beloved earworm started as a bar bet. December 1951, Reykhólar farm — the manager Sigurður Elíasson tells Sigfús he can't turn that poem into a tune in ten minutes. Ten minutes later: a national standard. Drinks were *not* on Sigurður.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **03 · Bláu augun** — *Haukur Morthens*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **04 · Vor við flóann** — *Ragnar Bjarnason*. Two-for-one. The 1959 7″ gives you Ragnar singing “Vor við flóann” on the A-side — flip it over and **Guðbergur Auðunsson** takes the mic for “Hvítir svanir.” Same record, two singers, no warning.  [Recorded somewhere unusual]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **05 · Æskuminning** — *Alfreð Clausen*. 1953. Iceland's first-ever ballad recorded with a full orchestra, Carl Billich on the baton. Walked it into the SKT dance-song competition the year before — and *lost*. The audience promptly overruled the judges and handed it the people's prize. Iceland figuring out who runs music: the people. Always the people.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **06 · Hæ Mambó** — *Haukur Morthens*. Yes — *that* Mambo Italiano. The Rosemary Clooney one. Loftur Guðmundsson Icelanded the lyrics and Reykjavík caught the mambo bug secondhand via 1950s Manhattan.  [Secret-cover thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **07 · Lilla Jóns** — *Guðbergur Auðunsson*. It's a Ray Sharpe rockabilly tune in Icelandic drag. Jón Sigurðsson took the American melody, dressed it in his own words, and out came “Little Jónsi.”  [Secret-cover thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **08 · Sveitapiltsins draumur** — *Hljómar*. California Dreamin'. With Icelandic lyrics. About a country boy. Yes, really.  [Secret-cover thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **09 · Sveitin milli sanda** — *Elly Vilhjálms*. There are no lyrics. None. Elly sings the entire thing on one open vowel — wordless, weightless, pure *Aaaaaa*. It started life as the score to a 1962 Ósvaldur Knudsen documentary; Magnús Blöndal Jóhannsson never bothered to add words and nobody ever asked.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **10 · Vor í Vaglaskógi** — *Vilhjálmur Vilhjálmsson*. Akureyri, February 1966. Two lovers go camping in Vaglaskógur — a 300-hectare birch forest in Fnjóskadalur — and Iceland gets its forever-song. The hook line every Icelander mouths on first beat: *Draumar þess rætast, sem gistir Vaglaskóg* — “the dreams of those who sleep in Vaglaskógur come true.” Kaleo dragged it onto the global stage in 2016. The forest has not stopped collecting tourists since.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **11 · Kling Klang** — *Dátar*. 1966 Keflavík teen-rock — fine. But the keyboard player? **Þórir Baldursson.** Twelve years later he'd be playing organ on Donna Summer, Giorgio Moroder and ABBA records. Pop is a small world. Iceland is an even smaller one.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **12 · If you knew** — *Thor's Hammer*. Recorded on Parlophone — *the Beatles' label* — in London, 1966. The “Umbarumbamba” EP that houses it now goes for thousands at auction; among 60s garage-rock collectors it's the white whale, the holy grail, the EP they'll remortgage their flat for.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **13 · Tætum og tryllum** — *Stuðmenn*. From the soundtrack of *Með allt á hreinu* (1982) — Iceland's biggest film of all time. 120,000 tickets. In a country of 230,000. Half the country watched it. Half the dialogue was improvised on the day, and the rival on-screen girl-band “Gærurnar” was actually Grýlurnar (skip ahead to track 19) — meaning the battle of the bands was real on screen *and* in the bar afterwards.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **ACT II — Finding the voice.** Iceland stops borrowing and starts getting copied. *Með allt á hreinu* eats half the country's box office — **120,000 tickets, 230,000 people**. Grýlurnar weaponise punk, and the band rivalry becomes the actual plot of the film. The Sugarcubes go global. Björk goes solo. GusGus turn out to be a twelve-person filmmaking collective who picked up instruments halfway through.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **14 · Reyndu aftur** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Mannakorn*. Track 2 of Mannakorn's January 1977 sophomore LP *Í gegnum tíðina*. The voice you're hearing? Pálmi Gunnarsson — same Pálmi who'd open Iceland's Eurovision account in Bergen 1986. Track 21 is also him. The man gets around.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **15 · Skólaball** — *Brimkló*. Plot twist confirmed by RÚV in 2021: *Skólaball er um stúlku sem síðar varð konan mín* — “the girl in the song became my wife.” Magnús Kjartansson met her at an actual school dance and wrote the actual song. The most romantic Reykjavík origin story that doesn't involve a horse.  [Song about someone]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **16 · Gáta dagsins** — *Spilverk þjóðanna*. Twenty seconds. *Twenty.* “Today's Riddle” clocks in shorter than a cigarette break — a deliberately cryptic micro-piece slipped in among the album's full-length songs. Blink and you've missed it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **17 · Á Sprengisandi** — *Þú og ég*. A 19th-century Grímur Thomsen *ghost poem* turned into a 1980 disco track. Yes. The placename comes from *sprengja* — “to ride a horse to death” — because the highland route was so brutal travellers were said to kill their mounts crossing it. Now picture that on a glitterball.  [Debut-LP opener]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **18 · Sísi** — *Grýlurnar*. It's not about anyone. The whole song is laughter and “vo-oh-oh”s and the name “Sísí” chanted as a hook — pure rhythm, no narrative. From *Mávastellið*, 1983. (The band's name means “the Grýlas” — Iceland's child-eating troll-mother, the lady who shows up at Christmas to scare your kids straight. Sweet branding.)  [Song about someone]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **19 · Svart-hvíta hetjan mín** — *Dúkkulísurnar*. Forty years and she still won't crack. Gréta Sigurjónsdóttir wrote both words and music in 1986 and Icelanders have been begging ever since: *who is the black-and-white hero?* Not telling. “Their best-kept secret.” Stop asking.  [Song about someone]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **20 · Þorparinn** — *Magnús Eiríksson, Pálmi Gunnarsson*. The song is about its own singer. Magnús Eiríksson watched his friend Pálmi Gunnarsson hauling fish in Vopnafjörður before fame found him — and wrote it down. The voice you're hearing is the voice of the song's own subject. Meta-loop activated.  [Song about someone]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **21 · Deus** — *The Sugarcubes*. “Deus does not exist… but if he does, he lives in the sky above me.” Sing-songed like a kindergarten chant. Delivered in fluent Icelandic blasphemy. Whole band straight-faced through the entire thing. The Sugarcubes never did anything halfway.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **22 · Venus As A Boy – 7″ Dream Mix** — *Björk, Mick Hucknall, Gota Yashiki*. Now for the most-WTF production credit on this entire playlist — the 1993 “Dream Mix” was produced by **Mick Hucknall.** As in: Simply Red. As in: *Holding Back the Years* Mick Hucknall. He had a side production company called Dream that year and Björk used it. Pop is so weird.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **23 · Lög unga fólksins** — *Unun*. Title nicked straight from RÚV — *Lög unga fólksins* is Iceland's long-running pop-request show, “Songs of Young People.” Naming your 1994 alt-rock single after the state-broadcast request show is the indie equivalent of calling your album *Top of the Pops*.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **24 · Oh – Edit** — *GusGus*. Hidden inside this slick Reykjavík club banger: a 1959 *tiki-bar* instrumental. Hawaiian exotica composer Arthur Lyman's “Taboo Tu,” sampled in. GusGus reached back forty years and pulled out a luau.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **25 · Sá ég spóa** — *Savanna tríóið*. Authorship: nobody. It's a *þjóðlag* — an anonymous Icelandic folk song that Savanna tríóið nailed down in the now-definitive arrangement. The lyric is twelve seconds of pocket-sized natural history: a curlew on the marsh, a golden plover singing “bí-bí-bí,” and that's it — that's spring, officially clocked in by the *lóa*.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **26 · Serenade** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Album closer of *Fisherman's Woman* (Rough Trade, 2005). Torrini said the entire album was “a letter I wrote to a person that I lost at that time. I coped by thinking I was with a fisherman.” Serenade is the dream-state final page of that letter — the bit where she lets him go.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **ACT I — Silence.** You have been awake since six and the whole day is in your bones. Piano, strings, glass-cool modern classical, and a lullaby to close it. That lullaby, track three, is — heads up — technically about infanticide. We will not dwell.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **01 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **02 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **03 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **ACT II — Eyes Open.** The warmth creeps in. Laufey waltzes. **Elín Hall** sings about her dad running *toward* the lava — not a metaphor, in a country built on the stuff. **Ásgeir's** actual father writes his son a song called *The Journey Home*, and the bus suddenly knows where it is going. Then BRÍET, Friðrik Dór and Jón Jónsson, and Valdimar lift it up off the floor.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **04 · Bewitched** — *Laufey*. Title track of the 2023 album that won Laufey the Grammy for Best Traditional Pop Vocal Album in 2024. She wrote it as a “guitar voice waltz” about the moment of falling helplessly into new love after a perfect first date — then asked the **Philharmonia Orchestra** to score the inside of her head. She calls it the song that “sets the sound of the album.” One song. One orchestra. One Grammy. Done.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **05 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **06 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **07 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **08 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **09 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **ACT III — Bags Packed.** Reykjavík widens ahead and the volume comes up. Of Monsters and Men, then **Una Stef** singing *Like Home* — her father wrote track 39 of the other playlist. Agent Fresco blow the doors off. Reykjavík's own mystery woman finally gets a name, seventy years late. Quarashi, and then **Ingó Veðurguð** has the last word.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **10 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **11 · Like Home** — *Una Stef*. Keep track 39 of the other playlist in mind. *Á Góðum Degi* is by **Stefán S. Stefánsson** — and Una Stef is his daughter. Two playlists, one family, and a song called *Like Home* arriving right as Reykjavík comes back into view. Neither of us planned that.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **12 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **13 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Friðrik Dór*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke. Friðrik Dór cut this reworking in **2016**; his melody line wanders a fair way from Jón Múli’s original.  [Family wrote it]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **14 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **15 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **16 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 1.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: One full-circle glance before the city: behind the cones lies **Elliðavatn** — and on a low spit in it, **Þingnes**, the only ground anyone has ever dug an assembly out of from this era: around **20 booth foundations** and a **judgement ring**, protected since **1930** as *the ancient Kjalarnesþing site*. Whether it really is the þing **Ari fróði** put on **Kjalarnes**, fourteen kilometres that way, nobody has ever proven — so you're leaving the Golden Circle past the country's first parliament grounds. Probably.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology
en: Most tectonic plate boundaries sit invisible under 2 km of ocean. Here, **you can stand on it, walk it, and drink from the cracks**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology
en: Forget the postcard version where you "touch two continents at once." **Þingvellir** sits on the **Mid-Atlantic Ridge**, and what you're standing in is a **seven-kilometre-wide graben** — a strip of valley floor **sinking between two fault walls** as the plates pull apart about **2 cm a year**, the speed your fingernails grow.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir / 🌍 Þingvellir Geology
en: The cracks have names — **Almannagjá**, the big one you walk through, is the **torn edge on the North American side**. The plates never touch here: the valley floor between the fault walls belongs to **neither continent** — it's the seam, still ripping. Filling it is **Þingvallavatn**, Iceland's largest natural lake.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur
en: In the 11th century the farm was home to **Teitur Ísleifsson** — son of **Ísleifur Gissurarson, Iceland's first bishop** — who ran a **famous school** at the farm (the *first*-school crown belongs to **Skálholt**). One of its boarders, from about **age seven**: **Ari fróði Þorgilsson** ("the Wise," c. 1067–1148), who grew up to write **Íslendingabók**, Iceland's foundational history and the reason we have any firm early dates at all.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Þingvellir → Haukadalur Valley / ⚖️ Haukadalur
en: But steam is only the valley's modern job: this was also a **chieftain's seat** — the home farm of the **Haukdælir**, one of the great power families of the Icelandic Commonwealth, with schoolmaster **Teitur Ísleifsson** as their patriarch.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: You are riding a snowmobile across a **1,400-metre-high freshwater reservoir that sits on two volcanoes and is quietly melting on a deadline.** Nowhere else does "just a bit of snow" carry that much backstory.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: We put you on a snowmobile on top of the very glacier that feeds every waterfall, geyser pool and fissure you've admired all day. Ride gently — you're on the source code.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: Snowmobiling on a Melting Giant

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: **Langjökull** means **"Long Glacier"** — Icelandic place-naming at its most ruthlessly literal, like nicknaming a tall bloke "Tall Man." It's **Iceland's second-largest ice cap** (after Vatnajökull): roughly **870–900 km²**, about **50 km long, up to 20 km wide**, holding on the order of **190 km³ of ice** up to **~580 m thick** and topping out just over **1,400 metres**. You'll be snowmobiling on more frozen water than most countries own.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: **Fire directly under the ice:** this isn't just frozen scenery — it's a **lid on two active volcanic systems**, **Prestahnúkur** and **Hveravellir**. The calm white surface you're carving across has a temper it simply hasn't used lately.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: **The waterworks of the whole Golden Circle:** Langjökull's meltwater feeds the **Hvítá** — the river that becomes **Gullfoss** — plus the **Ölfusá** system, and, via groundwater filtered through porous lava, the eerily clear **Silfra** fissure back at Þingvellir. Everything wet you've seen today drained off the glacier under your skis.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: **The timer:** Langjökull has been **losing mass steadily for decades**, and Institute of Earth Sciences modelling projects it could be **largely gone within about 150 years** on present warming — the fastest-shrinking of Iceland's big caps. Snowmobiling here is less "extreme sport," more "**visiting a patient you'll outlive.**"

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss / 🏔️ Langjökull
en: For the fully indoors version, the **"Into the Glacier"** ice tunnel — the world's largest man-made bore into a glacier, **~500 m** long, opened **1 June 2015** from the Húsafell side — lets you walk *inside* Langjökull past ice older than the settlement of Iceland. A museum you have to dig.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 2.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: The walls are **red scoria** — iron-rich basalt cinders whose iron has **oxidised to hematite**, rust essentially, helped along by groundwater; give it a few thousand more years and it'll blacken like its neighbours. The lake is **groundwater** (7–14 m deep) with **no inlet or outlet** — it just tracks the water table, turquoise because the water absorbs red light first against a dark floor. There's even life in it: a 2014 study found **10 kinds of zooplankton**.

en: The "Secret" Lagoon That Taught Iceland to Swim

ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin
en: **Gamla Laugin** ("the Old Pool") at **Hverahólmi** by Flúðir was **built in 1891** — **Iceland's oldest surviving swimming pool**, older than the national grid, the republic, and your great-grandparents. The "Secret Lagoon" branding was bolted on 120-odd years later; the water never went anywhere.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin
en: Before it was a pool it was a **parliament**: the local Flúðir assembly met on this exact patch until **1894**. Iceland's founding instinct, again — find a warm bit of ground and hold a vote on it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin
en: In **1909** it hosted **Iceland's first formal swimming lessons** — **32 men** in the debut course, girls following by **1911** — and taught the district every summer until **1947**. In a country ringed by a lethal North Atlantic, teaching the nation to swim in a hot bath was a genuinely brilliant life-hack.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin
en: Then it was **abandoned for nearly 70 years** — the village built a modern pool and left the old one to the algae. Scrubbed up and reborn on **7 June 2014**, history intact.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 3.0 / Gullfoss → Reykjavík / ♨️ Gamla Laugin
en: The water sits at **38–40°C year-round**, sulphur-rich, kept topped up **100% by the surrounding hot springs** — including a **baby geyser, Litli Geysir**, that fires every few minutes just off the deck. The one hot tub on Earth plumbed straight into a working geyser.

en: The lights? In **1921** they dammed it for **Elliðaárstöð** — **Reykjavík's first power station**, and by a wide margin the biggest in the country when it opened — switched on by King **Christian X** in person on **27 June 1921** and still running a century later.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Reykholt / Friðheimar / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Iceland's *actual* first hydro plant was humbler: in **1904** a Hafnarfjörður carpenter, **Jóhannes Reykdal**, wired a **9 kW** generator to his workshop stream and lit **15 houses — the school and the Good Templars' hall among them — plus four street lamps**: officially "Iceland's first power station," realistically a shed with big dreams.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Reykholt / Friðheimar / 🏞️ Elliðaárdalur
en: Upstream, on a low spit in **Elliðavatn** called **Þingnes**, sits the ground identified since **1841** as the **Kjalarnesþing** — **Iceland's first assembly**, held by **Þorsteinn Ingólfsson** (the first settler's son) before the national **Alþingi** of **930**. **Ari fróði** put that þing on **Kjalarnes**; the ruins are here, fourteen kilometres away, and nobody has ever closed the gap. The old ground now lies **partly underwater** since the river was dammed. Very Icelandic: invent democracy, mislay it, then flood it. (More on parliaments right at the end of the day — hold that thought.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Reykholt / Friðheimar / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: The lake is **groundwater** (7–14 m deep) with **no inlet or outlet** — it just tracks the water table, turquoise because the water absorbs red light first against a dark floor. There's even life in it: a 2014 study found **10 kinds of zooplankton**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Reykholt / Friðheimar / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: The walls are **red scoria** — iron-rich basalt cinders whose iron has **oxidised to hematite**, rust essentially, helped along by groundwater. It's so young the iron is **still rusting**; give it a few thousand more years and it'll blacken like its neighbours.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Reykholt / Friðheimar / 🎵 Grímsnes & Kerið
en: It sits in the **Grímsnes** volcanic field on the western rift — the northernmost of a four-crater row, and the product of **one of a dozen or so Grímsnes eruptions** that built the **Grímsneshraun** lava field. (No single big bang, then — this one was built up slowly, the way Iceland does most things.)

en: Just south of the Arctic you shouldn't be able to grow a tomato — so Iceland grows a big share of its own on volcano heat and skips the shipping.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Friðheimar / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: **Reykholt** ("smoky hill") in **Bláskógabyggð** is the village — a whole cluster of geothermal greenhouses (**Friðheimar, Espiflöt, Jarðarberjaland** — literally "strawberry land," and more). **Friðheimar** is the headliner: a working tomato greenhouse where you eat lunch **among the vines**, soup ladled three feet from the plant that grew it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Friðheimar / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: The crop drinks the volcano: **~95°C geothermal water** piped straight from a borehole heats the glasshouse, **LED grow-lights** fake a summer through the black winter, and the vines fruit **12 months a year — about 370 tonnes**, roughly **a tonne a day**, a serious slice of every Icelandic tomato. The same volcanic heat that warms Reykjavík's living rooms, just aimed at lunch.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Friðheimar / 🍅 Reykholt & Friðheimar
en: No native insect can pollinate a tomato flower this far north, so Friðheimar **flew in Dutch bumblebees** — a striped workforce knocking out **up to 2,000 flowers a day**. Iceland outsourced its pollination department to the Netherlands and never looked back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Geysir → Þingvellir / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn
en: Neighbour lake **Apavatn** ("Marsh Lake") is where the "cold politics" happened. In **spring 1238**, during the Sturlung Age, **Sturla Sighvatsson** (Sturlungar) ambushed and captured his rival **Gizur Þorvaldsson** (Haukdælir) right here — forcing him to swear on the Bible to give up power and sail to Norway.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 4.0 / Geysir → Þingvellir / 🛁 Laugarvatn & Apavatn
en: Gizur had his fingers crossed. He broke the oath, teamed up with **Kolbeinn ungi**, and five months later — **~1,700 men against ~1,000** — crushed the Sturlungar at **Örlygsstaðir (21 August 1238)**, the largest battle ever fought on Icelandic soil. Sturla's ancient family spear **Grásíða kept bending in his hands** as the tide turned; Gizur is said to have struck the fatal blow. So much for hot-tub diplomacy at the lake next door.

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm in **Meðalland**, right here in south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered out east to **Borgarfjörður eystri**; too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: The crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, the fishermen's union topped it up. **1911**: he tried **London** — the **Royal Academy slammed the door**. The rejection was the redirect: **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: Home again, he painted Iceland like no-one had — knelt over the **moss and lava three inches from his nose**, and swore he saw **elves and hidden folk** in the cracks. (In Iceland, that's not a diagnosis. That's a career.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: In **1968** he handed the city a huge part of everything he owned — the museum's Kjarval collection runs to **thousands of works** — and he died **owning almost nothing.** The grey block in Klambratún is **Kjarvalsstaðir**, Iceland's **first purpose-built art museum** (1973); since **1995** his face is on the **2,000-króna note** — the only cod fisherman ever **promoted to legal tender.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: **1913**: **Tómas Tómasson** starts Ölgerðin in a Reykjavík basement — at first just **malt extract** — and names it after **Egill Skallagrímsson**, the Viking warrior-poet who could spin stunning verse and drink a whole hall under the table.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: Two years later Iceland bans **all alcohol** (1915). Wine creeps back in 1922, spirits in 1935 — but **beer stays illegal until 1989**. Why beer alone? It was seen as **Danish**, and sipping a Danish lager while fighting Denmark for independence felt like treason.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: So Ölgerðin cheats: brews **Egils Pilsner kept just under the legal 2.25%** — beer that technically wasn't beer. A loophole in a glass. (The orange **Appelsín** everyone drowns in malt at Christmas? That came later — **1955**.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: The irony: Ölgerðin became a **purveyor to the Danish royal court** under King **Christian X** — a Danish royal warrant, in a country half-banning beer for being too Danish.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏢 Ölgerðin Egill Skallagrímsson
en: Real beer finally returned **1 March 1989** — now **Bjórdagurinn, "Beer Day."** Egils didn't fight for shelf space; they already owned it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: Just before the cones, that shallow lake on the right is **Rauðavatn**, “Red Water” — and the scruffy belt of trees beside it is the **oldest deliberate woodland in the Reykjavík area**. In **1901** around eighty shareholders founded **Skógræktarfélag Reykjavíkur**, bought **six hectares** by the lake, and put the Danish forester **C. E. Flensborg** in charge of the summers. (How do you find your way out of an Icelandic forest? Stand up. This is where somebody first tried to ruin that joke.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / ⛰️ Rauðhólar
en: **Ari the Wise** wrote in *Íslendingabók* that at settlement Iceland was **viði vaxið milli fjalls og fjöru** — wooded from the mountains to the shore; today woodland covers about **1.5% of the country.** They dug **8,600 holes** here in **1902** and planted about **8,000 rowan** the next summer — frost killed nearly all of it, and the fence never held (a newspaper in **1918** grumbled that the livestock **gengur þar inn og út**, in and out as they pleased). Only after the Second World War, with **close to 60,000 plants**, did it stick. The oldest **mountain pines** by the lake are now **over 100 years old** — a national repair job running since 1901.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: Hveragerði sits directly on the **Hengill volcanic system**. On **29 May 2008** the ground threw a **doublet**: Veðurstofa announced a **6.3** that afternoon; the papers later showed it was **two quakes three seconds apart** — **Mw 5.8 under Ingólfsfjall** and **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault five kilometres west** — **composite Mw 6.1**. It opened new hot springs in gardens and split buildings.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: Rather than hide it, locals built the **Quake 2008** exhibition inside the shopping centre — stand on the actual floor fissure and ride a shaking simulator.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: The hot ground makes it the **greenhouse capital** of the north: geothermal tomatoes, cucumbers, flowers — and the famous **bananas**. Myth-bust: the agricultural school planted those around **1950** as an *experiment*, and they were **never commercial**. Iceland is not, and never was, a banana republic.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: For scale: **about 140 people at the end of 1941**, **about 400 by 1946** — the year the district was formally constituted — and **about 3,350 today (3,344 at the start of 2026).** The name is far older than the town. **Hveragerði first appears in Fitjaannáll shortly before 1700**, in an account of an erupting hot spring that **shifted position during earthquakes in 1597**, and by the description of Ölfus written in **1703** the springs were already in daily use for **bathing, boiling and washing.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: Veðurstofa Íslands logged that quake to the minute — **fimmtudaginn 29. maí kl. 15:45**, epicentre at **Ingólfsfjall in Ölfus, about 5 km north-west of Selfoss**, with a very large number of aftershocks behind it. (Two quakes, one bang; nobody in town stopped to count.) And the best thing in **Sunnumörk** was never meant to be an exhibit at all: when the centre was under construction in **2003** an **earthquake fissure was found in the ground beneath it**, and instead of filling it in they **lit it and left it on show.** **Admission is free** — you pay only if you want a turn in the simulator, which runs at **over 6 on the Richter scale.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🏡 Keldur
en: In **1932** a hidden **underground tunnel** was found running from the hall down toward a stream — not romantic, purely practical: an **escape route** if enemies tried to torch the house with everyone asleep inside. Saga-age arson was a known hazard, not a plot device.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: Just after midnight on **23 January 1973** a **1.6 km fissure** tore open at the edge of town on **Heimaey**, and a brand-new volcano — **Eldfell**, "Fire Mountain" — began throwing lava through the eastern half of the streets.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: The lucky break was weather: a storm the day before had kept the whole **fishing fleet in harbour**, so of about **5,300 residents, roughly 5,000 were evacuated in around eight hours** — Iceland has **no army**, so the fishermen ran the evacuation themselves.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: The eruption ran **five months** and buried about **400 buildings**. To save the harbour, crews pumped **millions of litres of North Atlantic seawater** onto the advancing lava for weeks — and the cooled flow left the entrance **deeper and more sheltered than before.**

ctx: gloss for the name "Vestmannaeyjar" — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🐦 Vestmannaeyjar
en: the Westman Islands out to sea on the right, nearly wiped off the map in 1973

en: "There's nothing here," they say. Under you: old seabed. Ahead: glacial wash-plain. Left: ghost coastline. That's a lot of nothing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
en: The name gives it away: **Landeyjar means "land islands"** — grassy patches that stood up out of the marsh and sand. Waves once rolled over where this road runs, the sea reaching right up to that **cliff line on your left**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains
en: Then the land rose, the rivers kept dumping sand, and the coastline **marched south, kilometre by kilometre** — the shore is now several km further out than the cliffs that used to be beach.

ctx: gloss for the name "Landeyjar" — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌊 Landeyjar Plains

ctx: the spoken close — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: Out there: grass and sheep. In the sagas: a man who chose his view over his life — and didn't survive the choice.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: The Hero's Choice

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: In front of you, the **Markarfljót** runs **~100 km** to the sea, fed by two ice caps — **Mýrdalsjökull** and **Eyjafjallajökull** — that both sit on live volcanoes, which is why it has a temper. In **2010** engineers **deliberately breached the Ring Road embankment** to let the Eyjafjallajökull meltwater flood through and **save the bridge.** Sacrifice the road to keep the crossing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: Tucked into the far slopes is **Hlíðarendi**, home of **Gunnar** of **Njáll's saga** — the best of the saga heroes.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: Sentenced to exile, Gunnar rode out, looked back and said the line every Icelander knows: *"Fair is the hillside… I will not go away."*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi
en: That one glance cost him everything: he **turned back**, stayed, and was killed defending his farm.

ctx: gloss for the name "Markarfljót" — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🛡️ Markarfljót & Hlíðarendi

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: The Cloud That Stopped Europe

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: **Eyjafjallajökull** — an **~800,000-year-old** stratovolcano, summit **1,651 m**, under an ice cap now shrunk to about **66 km²** — sits there looking like a tidy white lid over green fields.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: By volcanic standards **2010 was small: a VEI 4, only ~0.27 km³ of ash.** But it fired a **plume 8–9 km high** straight into the **jet stream** — and the glassy particles turn jet engines into **expensive sandblasters.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: Result: the **worst aviation shutdown in Europe since WWII** — **104,000 flights cancelled over eight days, 15–22 April**, about **48% of expected European traffic**, leaving roughly **10 million passengers unable to fly**, with airspace over some **20 countries** closed. Europe learned volcanoes don't read timetables.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: At farms like **Þorvaldseyri** right at its foot, **500–800 people were evacuated overnight** as meltwater poured off the ice; farmers **milked cows in respirator masks** and scraped ash off the roofs — then built a small visitor centre, because if a volcano rewrites your year you may as well sell the story.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: Guest question, every time: does it trigger **Katla** next door? Historically the 920, 1612 and 1821 eruptions each were — but in **2010 Katla stayed shut.** Eyjafjallajökull is a **warning light, not a trigger.**

ctx: gloss for the name "Eyjafjallajökull" — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull
en: the glacier volcano whose 2010 ash cloud grounded European air travel

ctx: gloss for the name "Þorvaldseyri" — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🌋 Eyjafjallajökull

en: A single stone that lets you flip between two ways of seeing Iceland — geology and saga — at the same time.

en: Geologists see a subglacial tuff plug. Storytellers see a giant's bite mark on a rock that never finished becoming gravel.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: The Stone That Stayed

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: **Drangurinn** stands alone in the field like a stubborn leftover — a block of **palagonite tuff (móberg)**, the same subglacial-eruption rock that built nearby **Pétursey**, left behind when the softer cliff around it eroded away. Farmers were so unbothered they used it as a **natural barn**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: The saga version: **Grettir the Strong** — Iceland's great troublemaking outlaw — supposedly tore the rock from the mountain and hurled it here, leaving a **bite-mark notch in the ridge above**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Hvolsvöllur → Sólheimajökull / 🪨 Drangurinn
en: Once you know the story, that notch stops looking like erosion and starts looking like a **missing tooth**. And a boulder this dramatic naturally comes with **elf traditions** — recorded in **Jón Árnason's folktales** — and a film career: it starred in the Viking film *Hrafninn flýgur* ("When the Raven Flies").

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: A gravel path pulls you toward **Sólheimajökull**, an outlet tongue of **Mýrdalsjökull** — **Iceland's 4th-largest ice cap** — wedged neatly between the volcanoes **Katla** and **Eyjafjallajökull**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: In front sits a **blue-green proglacial lagoon** with small icebergs calving off; the colour is **glacial flour**, rock ground so fine it turns the water to liquid stone-dust.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull / 🧊 Sólheimajökull
en: The tongue is **retreating around 40 m a year** — a bus-length of ice a summer. Signs along the path mark where the front *used* to reach: "here… and here… and here." You've just walked **decades of retreat in a few minutes.**

ctx: the point of the block — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: It's a **modern layer on the geology**: Katla built the sandur, the Americans accidentally parked a plane on it, and social media did the rest.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: From the bus, you mostly see empty blackness. The drama is the crew who glided this thing engine-out into the middle of nowhere — and all seven lived.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: The Ghost in the Sand

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: On **21 November 1973** a **US Navy Douglas C-117D** — a beefed-up "Super DC-3," though everyone insists on calling it a plain DC-3 — was flying **Höfn to Keflavík** when **both engines choked on carburettor ice over Vatnajökull.** Myth-bust: it did **not** "run out of fuel."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: The co-pilot turned the powerless plane — "a massively overweight glider" — **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the bare hull.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: For decades a quiet local landmark; then **Justin Bieber** (2015) and the Bollywood hit *Dilwale* filmed here and **Instagram** did the rest. Today visitors walk a **4 km track each way** — the road was closed to cars in **2016** — across old ocean floor just to touch a wingless plane in a volcanic desert.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: Not a joke in bad weather: the plain has **no shelter at all**, and **two visitors died of hypothermia** near the wreck in a January 2020 storm.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: 🎬 **On screen:** This lonely wreck is a music-video magnet — **Justin Bieber's** "I'll Show You" (2015), Sigur Rós's *Heima* documentary (2007), and Bollywood's *Dilwale* ("Gerua") all used the plane and the black desert around it.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: **Pétursey** ("Peter's Island") is **móberg** — the ash-and-rubble palagonite rock formed when a volcano **erupts under ice or sea** in the last Ice Age; hot magma met cold water, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls. Same recipe as nearby **Drangurinn**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: Its old name was literally **"Tall Island"** — because for much of the Holocene the Atlantic really did surround it and sailors used it as a **landmark**, until **Katla**'s black sand slowly filled the gap and tethered it to the mainland.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: In the **Sturlungaöld** civil war, some **200 armed men fortified the summit** as a defensible keep — a 360° view and one way up.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: The cliffs still work as a **seabird colony** — fulmars and **puffins** circle it as if it never stopped being an island — and, this being Iceland, the mound is thick with **hidden-folk and elf legends**. At the base today: two farms, **Eystri-** and **Vestri-Pétursey**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: His son **Guðjón Samúelsson** grew up here and became **Iceland's State Architect** — the man behind **Hallgrímskirkja**, the basalt-column church on the Reykjavík hill, *and* the concrete lighthouse out at **Dýrhólaey** we'll pass.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: Hallgrímskirkja was **commissioned in 1937** but took a marathon to build — finally **consecrated in 1986, 36 years after Guðjón died in 1950.** He never saw his own masterpiece finished.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / ⛪ Skeiðflatarkirkja
en: You can feel these **simple, sturdy rural churches**, built to shrug off wind, rain and ash, echoing in the capital's skyline — Iceland's grandest church is a farm chapel that went to architecture school.

en: A teaching stop par excellence: glacial plains, old islands and active coastal erosion all visible in **one slow spin of your head**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: **Dýrhólaey** ("door-hill island") formed about **100,000 years ago** in a **submarine eruption**, then waves hammered a huge natural **sea arch** through it — the "door" of the name — under **~100 m cliffs**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: On top sits a castle-like lighthouse: Iceland's **first landfall light and its brightest**, visible **43 km (27 nautical miles)** out to sea — first tower 1910, the concrete one **1927 by Guðjón Samúelsson**, the same architect as the church a few stops back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Sólheimajökull → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: Long called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it **for several decades**, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Under that ice sits **Katla** — a **~10 km-wide caldera**, summit **1,512 m** — one of Iceland's biggest, angriest volcanoes. The cap above is **Mýrdalsjökull**, Iceland's **4th-largest ice cap** — **520 km² as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890** — acting as a several-hundred-metre insulating blanket over a furnace.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: She's produced **at least 21 eruptions in the last 1,100 years**, typically **VEI 4–5** — bigger than famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last one to come up through the ice, **1918**, ran **24 days** and dumped so much flood sediment — **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand** — that it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** A volcano that does land reclamation.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: The gaps between her eruptions have run from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — and it is now **108 years since 1918, the longest quiet spell on record.** (Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Erupting under ice, she produces a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has drilled for this for decades.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: In **1918 Katla** erupted under the ice and sent a **jökulhlaup** to sea so vast it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km**, burying everything under fresh sand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: To the east, **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once sat by open sea — is now stranded **inland**, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black sand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: Odd bragging rights: **Vík shares the title of Iceland's warmest weather station with Vestmannaeyjar** — around **5.9 °C** a year on the recent normals. It's also **one of the wettest inhabited places in Iceland** — about **2,330 mm** a year, roughly triple Reykjavík. The actual record-holder is **Kvísker**, out east under Öræfajökull, which took **4,630 mm in 2002 alone.** The church above town is the official "**run here if Katla wakes**" point.

ctx: the point of the block — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Iceland's history didn't start with peace. It started with **blood feuds** — and a vengeful housekeeper who lives in the ice.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Most countries' founding stories are statues and speeches. Iceland's is a body, a brother, and a witch in a skyr-vat.

ctx: subtitle under the block title — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Blood-Brother and Witch-in-the-Ice

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **221 m palagonite (móberg) inselberg** named after **Hjörleifur Hróðmarsson**, the sworn **blood-brother** of Iceland's first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson**.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Per *Landnámabók*, Hjörleifur settled here around **874** and, **within a year (c. 875)**, was **murdered by his own enslaved Irish/Hebridean men** — one of the very few slave revolts the sagas record. Ingólfur tracked them to the islands on the horizon and killed them in revenge.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Here's the payoff on the map: those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar** — the **"Isles of the West Men."** *Vestmenn* was the Norse word for the **Gaels of Ireland and the Hebrides** — so the archipelago out there is **named after the enslaved Gaels themselves.** The romantic image of free, self-made Viking farmers is missing a chapter.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: At its base sits **Kötluklettur**, "Katla's Rock." The tale: **Katla**, a housekeeper at nearby **Þykkvabæjarklaustur** with **magic breeches** that made her run impossibly fast, killed the shepherd boy **Barði** for borrowing them and hid him in a **vat of skyr** — then, as the whey dropped and discovery loomed, threw herself into the glacier. Every eruption, they say, is her ghost. **The volcano is named after her.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Like Pétursey, this cape **was once an island**, now tethered to the coast by miles of Katla's black sand.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: The **Skógá river** skips the rapids and walks straight off the old sea-cliff — a clean **60 m drop, 25 m wide** — free-falling into a deep pool before racing across the sandur to the Atlantic.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: At the base you have to **shout to be heard** — which is why most videos from here are people silently pointing. The metal staircase on the right is your free fitness test; at the top begins the **Fimmvörðuháls trail**, which climbs the river **between Eyjafjallajökull and Mýrdalsjökull** — the same gap the 2010 eruption first cracked open.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: This cliff is the **coastline of thousands of years ago**: textbook waterfall geology — hard cap-rock over soft, undercut and collapsing, so the fall eats **upstream** and leaves a gorge behind it. The land then lifted, rivers dumped black sand, and the real shore marched several km south — Skógafoss never moved.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: Behind the car park: **Skógar Museum** (turf houses, old church, farm buildings) and a **bonus waterfall, Kvernufoss**, hiding in a green gorge next door. Plus the legend of **Þrasi's treasure** — a settler's gold chest hidden behind the falls; would-be looters snapped off the iron ring, which ended up on the **church door**. The gold did not follow.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 5.0 / Skógafoss / 🏞️ Skógafoss
en: 🎬 **On screen:** The big one for filmmakers — *Thor: The Dark World* (2013), *Vikings* (Floki's storyline, Season 5), a *Game of Thrones* aerial sequence in the final season, the old *Beowulf & Grendel* (2005), India's *Dilwale*, *Aadhavan* and *Namo Venkatesa* — and yes, **Justin Bieber** clambered up it for his "I'll Show You" video.

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** farm in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **"Jói í Geitavík."** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🧍 Jóhannes Sveinsson Kjarval
en: The crew saw his sketches, **passed the hat**, and the labour union topped it up. **1911**: he tried **London** — the **Royal Academy slammed the door**. The rejection was the redirect: **1912** he reached **Copenhagen** and the **Royal Danish Academy** (graduated **1917**).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / 🌋 Hveragerði
en: On **29 May 2008** the ground threw a **doublet** — **Mw 5.8 beneath Ingólfsfjall**, then **Mw 5.9 on the Kross fault about 5 km to the west**, the two starting **within 3 seconds of each other** for a **composite Mw 6.1** — and shook the town with ground acceleration up to **0.88 g** (near 1 g, the earth is shoving as hard as gravity). Rather than hide it, locals built the **Quake 2008** exhibition **on top of the fissure it opened**, crack left showing.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: Everyone calls it a "DC-3." It isn't. It's a **US Navy Super DC-3 (a Douglas R4D-8 / C-117D)** — same family, buff cousin who went to the gym. It's worn the wrong name for fifty years like a stag-do lanyard.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: On **21 November 1973** it was flying from **Höfn to Keflavík** when **ice choked both carburettors over the Vatnajökull ice cap** and both engines quit. The tourist story that it "ran out of fuel" is false — it iced up and became, in the co-pilot's words, "a massively overweight glider."

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: The pilot turned **south for the coast** and put it down on the black sand. **All seven crew walked away.** The Navy stripped the useful parts and left the shell.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck
en: For decades it was a quiet local landmark; then a **Bieber video (2015)** and Instagram turned it into a pilgrimage. Cars were banned in **2016**, so now you walk **4 km each way** across old ocean floor just to touch a plane with no wings.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ✈️ The DC-3 Wreck

en: **Pétursey** is **móberg** — ash-and-rubble rock formed when a volcano **erupted underwater** in the last Ice Age; hot magma met cold sea, shattered mid-blast, and cemented into these steep walls.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey
en: For much of the Holocene the Atlantic surrounded it and it was a true **island** and sailors' landmark — until **Katla**'s black sand slowly swallowed the gap and stranded it inland.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / ⛰️ Pétursey

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: **Dýrhólaey** was born underwater ~**100,000 years ago** in a submarine eruption — half tuff (**Háey**), half basalt (**Lágey**) — then hammered by waves into a huge natural **sea arch**. In **October 1993** a pilot flew a small plane clean through it **three times** (once could've been luck).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: On top sits a **castle-like lighthouse** — Iceland's **first landfall light and brightest**, seen **43 km** out to sea; the current 1927 tower was designed by state architect **Guðjón Samúelsson** (yes — the same man behind that little church back down the road, and Hallgrímskirkja).

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: From the top you can read the whole **Katla Corridor** — the sandur behind, the **Reynisdrangar** needles ahead, and the Atlantic hurling itself at the basalt. Parts close in summer for **nesting puffins**: this is a full **seabird city**, a **protected reserve since 1978** under **100 m cliffs** — the birds were here first, and the reserve rules say so.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: The flyers have names: pilot **Arngrímur Jóhannsson** and MP **Árni Johnsen**, who took a light aircraft through the arch in **October 1993** — three passes, to prove the first wasn't luck.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: The name is literal: **Dýrhólaey** means **door-hill island** — the hill with the doorway through it. The first light went up here in **1910**; the tower you can see replaced it in 1927.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Skógafoss → Reynisfjara / 🚪 Dýrhólaey
en: Footnote for the pedants: it's long been called the **southernmost point of the mainland** — until **Katla's 1918 flood built Kötlutangi**, which took the title off it **for several decades**, before the sea carried that sand west again. The volcano moved the goalposts; the Atlantic moved them back.

en: The serious bit stays serious: the **sneaker waves here have killed at least five people since 2007**, with another death in 2025, which is why the **traffic-light warning system** went in in 2022. The folklore is the safer attraction.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Under that ice sits **Katla**: a **caldera ~10 km across**, summit **1,512 m**, hidden beneath **Mýrdalsjökull** — **520 km² of ice as measured in 2019**, down from about **607 km² around the year 2000** and **736 km² at its Little Ice Age peak around 1890.** Being subglacial is the whole danger — she doesn't just throw ash, she **flash-melts the glacier into floods.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: She's erupted **at least 21 times in the last 1,100 years**, with gaps running from **about 13 years to about 80, averaging just under 50** — usually bigger than her famous neighbour Eyjafjallajökull's 2010 show. The last eruption up through the ice — **1918** — lasted **24 days** and dumped **about 200 million m³ (0.2 km³) of sand**, pushing **the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km.** The volcano literally added land.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: It is now **108 years since 1918 — the longest quiet spell on her record.** She even leaks CO₂ while dormant — one study put her among **Earth's biggest volcanic CO₂ sources.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: Her system also produced **Eldgjá**, which began in the **spring of 939 CE** and ran on, at least episodically, into the **autumn of 940** — one of the largest lava floods of the last 2,000 years. When this family goes big, it goes very big.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Reynisfjara → Vík / 🌋 Katla
en: An eruption under ice makes a **jökulhlaup** — a glacial flood that can push **up to ~300,000 m³ a second** to the sea, faster than a galloping horse. The town ahead, **Vík**, has been drilling for this for decades.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: Vík shares the title of **Iceland's warmest weather station** with **Vestmannaeyjar** — around **5.9 °C** a year on the recent normals. It's also **one of the wettest inhabited places in Iceland** — about **2,330 mm** a year, roughly **triple Reykjavík**. (The actual record-holder is **Kvísker**, out east under Öræfajökull, which took **4,630 mm in 2002** alone.) "Warmest" is doing heroic work in that sentence.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🏘️ Vík í Mýrdal
en: In **1918 Katla** erupted under the ice and sent a **jökulhlaup** to sea so vast it **pushed the shore south of Hjörleifshöfði out by more than 3 km**, burying everything under fresh sand. To the east, **Hjörleifshöfði** — a saga headland that once sat by open sea — is now stranded inland, the gap quietly filled by a century of Katla's black sand.

ctx: the spoken close — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Most countries' founding stories are statues and speeches. Iceland's is a body, a fake bear, and a witch in a skyr-vat.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: **Hjörleifshöfði** is a **221 m móberg cape** named after **Hjörleifur**, the **blood-brother** of Iceland's first settler **Ingólfur Arnarson.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 6.0 / Vík í Mýrdal / 🛡️ Hjörleifshöfði
en: Around **875 CE** Hjörleifur forced his enslaved Irishmen to **drag his plough** like oxen; they killed his one ox, **blamed a bear** — and it worked, because Iceland *has no bears* and the newcomers didn't know that yet. When the men scattered to hunt the imaginary bear, the thralls murdered them and fled to the islands offshore. Ingólfur tracked them down and killed them; those islands are the **Vestmannaeyjar**, the "Isles of the West Men," named for the very Irishmen who did the deed.

en: Born **15 October 1885** at **Efri-Ey** in **Meðalland**, south Iceland — **9th of 13 kids** (his parents clearly had stamina). Fostered east to **Geitavík** in **Borgarfjörður eystri**, where the fjord still calls him **“Jói í Geitavík.”** Too poor for paint, he drew with **calf blood, soot and wool dye** — then went to sea.

The bishop refused to bless it — **too many elves, not enough Jesus** — so it still hangs there, gloriously **unconsecrated**. A second altarpiece, dismissed as “crude and ugly,” was bought by **Halldór Laxness** for **Gljúfrasteinn** (we pass it later). One man, two altarpieces, **zero bishops convinced.**

en: At peak tension a messenger reported **lava flowing on Hellisheiði**. Pagans cried “the gods are angry!”

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Kristnitökuhraun
en: Chieftain **Snorri Goði** pointed at the ancient lava underfoot: *“What were the gods angry about when this rock was made?”* Silence — and Iceland chose Christianity to keep **one law** for the whole island. *(Kristni saga)*

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Kristnitökuhraun
en: The field is the fresh top of the three-flow **Svínahraun** stack, radiocarbon-dated to around **1000 CE** — so it **inherited its name** from the conversion it coincided with. Fitting footnote: today the **CarbFix** project uses this very basalt to turn CO₂ into stone — the rock that once “proved” divine anger now mops up industrial emissions.

ctx: gloss for the name "Kristnitökuhraun" — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Kristnitökuhraun
en: the Christianity Lava on your right, named for the conversion it coincided with

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: Via **CarbFix**, CO₂ is dissolved in water and pumped into hot basalt, where **~95% turns to solid rock within about two years** (Matter et al., 2016). Next door, **Climeworks' “Mammoth”** plant (2024) sucks CO₂ straight from the air — up to **36,000 tonnes a year** — for the same rock treatment.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Hellisheiðarvirkjun
en: While the world debates carbon capture, Iceland dissolves the problem in water, files it under “rocks,” and moves on.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: Only **~25 km long**, yet **Iceland's largest river by discharge** — about **400 m³ every second** off a **~5,760 km² basin**. Not the longest; just the one you absolutely could not cross.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: It follows the **South Iceland Seismic Zone**, zig-zagging along fault lines. Beside it lies **Þjórsárhraun** — about **8,700 years** old, roughly **1,000 km²**, the **longest lava flow in Iceland**. Vísindavefur puts it higher than that (id=87471, Haraldur Sigurðsson, January 2025): *“Þjórsárhraun er stærsta hraun sem runnið hefur á jörðinni síðan ísöldinni lauk”* — the largest lava flow to have run anywhere on Earth since the Ice Age ended.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: For centuries the **ultimate obstacle**: unfordable, no bridge, just a ferry at **Laugardælir** paid in **cattle or cod** to reach the harbour at **Eyrarbakki**. When it flooded catastrophically in **1623**, a bishop blamed a giant river serpent — an “ice worm.” (It was an **ice-jam flood**; the serpent just got the better press.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: That lava has a proper name and a frankly silly scale: **Þjórsárhraunið mikla**, the Great Þjórsá Lava. It erupted **about 8,700 years ago** from a **fissure 20 to 30 km long** in the **Veiðivötn swarm of the Bárðarbunga system**, well up in the interior, then ran **about 130 km to the sea**, reaching the coast **between the Þjórsá and the Ölfusá.** Total volume: **25 cubic kilometres.**

ctx: fact bullet — tour 7.0 / BSÍ Bus Terminal → Hvolsvöllur / Ölfusá
en: On the magnitude scale Vísindavefur rates it **MS-9 — the largest Icelandic eruption by volume of erupted material** — ahead of **Eldgjá at MS-8** and a long way ahead of **Laki 1783 at MS-6.5.** That scale is logarithmic, so the gaps are wider than they look. Keep one distinction straight, though: largest by volume is not the same as **most powerful**, and that title goes to **Eldgjá**. The same system gave us **Vatnaöldur in 871** and **Veiðivötn in 1477.** (The biggest eruption this island ever produced is shaped like a field. You cannot see it, and that is exactly how large it is.)
