en: Through Borgarnes — my own playlist from here to BSÍ.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **01 · Sofðu unga ástin mín** — *Hafdís Huld*. Heads up — Iceland's most beloved lullaby is, technically, *about infanticide*. The lyric is from Jóhann Sigurjónsson's 1911 play *Fjalla-Eyvindur*: outlaw's wife Halla sings it to her own baby seconds before throwing the child into a waterfall so she and her fugitive husband can keep running across the highlands. Icelandic parents have nonetheless been singing this to their toddlers ever since. Hafdís Huld cut this version on *Vögguvísur* (2012) at home — while pregnant with her own daughter Arabella. Sleep tight, kids.  [Lullaby thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **02 · Flight from the City** — *Jóhann Jóhannsson*. Opening track of *Orphée* (2016) — Jóhann's first solo album for Deutsche Grammophon, and the last solo album he ever made before he died in Berlin in February 2018. The whole record traces the Orpheus myth — death, rebirth, looking back — and was tied directly to his own move from Copenhagen to Berlin. *Flight from the City* is the literal opening of that journey out. Listen to it knowing he never made another.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **03 · Bambaló (feat. Steiney Sigurðardóttir)** — *Gabríel Ólafs*. Plot twist — that “traditional Icelandic lullaby” is actually an *Irish* folk tune that hitchhiked north centuries ago. The word *bambaló* is essentially Icelandic for “rock-a-bye.” Gabríel cut this version with cellist Steiney Sigurðardóttir for *Lullabies for Piano and Cello*. Iceland: still wearing imported clothes, still pulling it off.  [Lullaby thread]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **05 · Twice** — *Little Dragon*. The piano line you're hearing wasn't supposed to be a Little Dragon song. It was written for a *children's collage book*. Yukimi Nagano walked into the studio, heard drummer Erik Bodin's friend's kids'-book melody, and started scribbling lyrics on the spot. It became Little Dragon's debut single (2007) and got them signed to Peacefrog. Robert Glasper Experiment later covered it. Bedtime story to indie classic, in one studio drop-by.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **06 · Pretty Face** — *Sóley*. Track 2 of Sóley's 2011 debut *We Sink*. The lyric obsesses over the narrator's own reflection in someone else's eyes — validation, identity, choosing to disappear into a dream rather than stay. Listen for the eerie under-hum; that's the song quietly unraveling around you.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **07 · Tachylite** — *Elín Hall*. *Tachylite* is volcanic glass — basaltic lava that cooled too fast to crystallise. Elín Hall calls it “failed lava.” The song is a quiet tribute to her father — an **Icelandic geophysicist who works as a first responder during eruptions**. He runs *toward* the lava. She wrote a song called Failed Lava about him. Released January 2026.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **08 · Heimförin** — *Ásgeir*. *The Journey Home.* The lyrics are by **Ásgeir's dad** — Einar Georg Einarsson, a poet from the village of Laugarbakki — and most of the original Icelandic words on the 2012 debut *Dýrð í dauðaþögn* are his father's. A song called The Journey Home, written by Dad, set to music and sung by son. The album went on to become the best-selling Icelandic debut *of all time*. Family business.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **09 · In Too Deep** — *BRÍET*. Bríet's debut single — self-released in 2018 when she was eighteen. She set out to write a happy love song and changed direction mid-write; the girl in the song starts smiling and ends pulled under. The track that introduced her voice internationally.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **10 · Á Sama Tíma, Á Sama Stað** — *Friðrik Dór & Jón Jónsson*. The brothers Jónsson. (Yes — actual brothers.) The song was the official 2018 *Þjóðhátíðarlag* — the festival anthem of Þjóðhátíð on the Westman Islands, where every August Iceland packs into a lava-walled valley called Herjólfsdalur and sings whatever song the year's commissioned writer hands them. 2018: the brothers' turn. The country's biggest weekend, scored by two siblings sharing a mic.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **11 · Á Flug** — *Valdimar*. *In Flight.* Valdimar are from **Keflavík** — i.e. the literal airport town this coach just left. From their 2010 debut *Undraland*, released on Geimsteinn, the Keflavík label founded by Rúnar Júlíusson. A song about flight, made by guys you flew over.  [Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **12 · Tuna in a Can** — *Of Monsters and Men*. Yes — the song is actually about **canned tuna**. The image — *tuna in a can, sticky from the brine / I thought I'd gone bad, you thought I was fine* — is reportedly Nanna's nod to her **mum's tuna salad**. It became the visual anchor of the entire 2025 album *All Is Love and Pain in the Mouse Parade*; the cover is built around it as “a quilt of familial stories.” Best self-portrait-as-expired-canned-fish in modern indie pop.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **13 · Coming Home** — *Sjonni's Friends*. Sjonni Brink wrote the music. **His wife Þórunn Erna Clausen wrote the lyrics.** So in effect, this is her words sung back to her. He was due to perform it in Iceland's Eurovision semi-final on 29 January 2011 — and died of a brain aneurysm on **17 January 2011, age 36**. Twelve days before the show. Six of his musician friends formed *Vinir Sjonna* / Sjonni's Friends to perform it in his place at Eurovision in Düsseldorf, finishing 20th with 61 points. The song's message — *never know when your time's up, so live and love hard* — was written before he died. Then performed after.  [Family wrote it · Homecoming]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **14 · Howls** — *Agent Fresco*. Track 6 of *Destrier* (2015) — the concept album frontman Arnór Dan Arnarson wrote after **two men attacked him late one night and left him with a broken eye socket and concussion**. The whole record is grief and adrenaline. *Howls* sits at the nostalgic end — *howls of youth, when life would run with lawless legs to race the sun* — the memory of pre-violence freedom the rest of the album is trying to claw back. (A *destrier* is the medieval warhorse bred for battle.)

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **15 · Fröken Reykjavík** — *Ríó Tríó / Stórsveit Reykjavíkur*. Music by **Jón Múli Árnason**, lyrics by his brother **Jónas** — the Árnason brothers wrote dozens of Iceland's most-loved mid-century standards together. For seventy-odd years nobody knew who the red-shoed woman walking down Austurstræti actually *was*. Mystery solved in 2023 — director Björn Brynjúlfur Björnsson revealed in *Vísir* that she was his mother, **Jóna Sigurjónsdóttir**. Reykjavík kept its secret for seven decades. Then it broke.  [Family wrote it]

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **16 · Jungle Drum** — *Emilíana Torrini*. Co-written with producer Dan Carey, released as a single in March 2009. The “ay-ay-ay” scat hook took it to **No. 1 in Germany, Austria and Belgium** — Torrini's biggest chart hit by a country mile — *after* it got used in the *Germany's Next Topmodel* finale. German rockabilly band The Baseballs covered it the same year. The whole lyric is a heartbeat-as-tribal-drum metaphor. Sometimes a giant pop hit really is just *ay-ay-ay*.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **17 · Mr. Jinx** — *Quarashi*. The earworm hook is sampled from a 1973 American soul cut — **New York City's “Sanity”** — laundered through Reykjavík rap. The song itself never blew up on charts (peaked No. 43 on Radio & Records Alternative). But its second life was sync money — scoring trailers and incidental music for *Alias*, *Smallville*, NBA on TNT (2003–2005), and Madden NFL 2003. Their other *Jinx* track “Stick 'Em Up” snagged the *2 Fast 2 Furious* trailer. Iceland's quiet sync goldmine.

ctx: fact bullet — tour 9.0 / Ytri-Tunga → Reykjavík / 🎧 Music Leg
en: **18 · Takk fyrir mig** — *Ingó Veðurguð*. The last word of the day, and it was written for a party that never happened. This was **Þjóðhátíðarlagið 2020** — the official song of Vestmannaeyjar’s Þjóðhátíð, the biggest weekend in the Icelandic calendar. Ingó wrote it (his brother took a hand in part of it), and then the 2020 festival was called off under gathering restrictions. A thank-you sung to a crowd that never got to turn up. It gets its crowd on this bus instead.  [Homecoming]

en: The name is **Kirkjufell — "church mountain"** — centuries older than television. *Game of Thrones* (seasons **6 and 7**) only ever calls it **"the mountain shaped like an arrowhead"** — a line in a script, not a name. Danish sailors called it **Sukkertoppen**, the sugar top. Church: original. Arrowhead: fan fiction. Sugar: the Danes were hungry.
